articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department hosted its eighth annual Car Show on Saturday, September 26, out front of the police station and also along Moraga and Highland Avenues. Event organizer and co-founder Officer Tyler Petit shepherded his last big community outreach event in his Piedmont Police blues, as he will turn in his uniform on Wednesday, September 30. For Petit, this event marked a victory lap; the event he spearheaded along with Sergeant Steve Dewarns in 2018 has quickly turned into a must attend event for local car enthusiasts. The coffee was hot and delicious, getting patrons’ engines revving in the 7 a.m. hour while the chrome was still heating up. Seemingly the entire police force was on hand, with uniformed officers on the street shaking hands and answering questions along with officers in street clothes there to support the community event whether on the clock or not. articles.text: Editor, I’m writing in support of Measure GG. Raising the city’s transfer tax to be more in line with our neighboring cities of Oakland and Berkeley is a reasonable way to raise the funds necessary to fund city services and projects. As a long-serving member and current Chair of the Parks Commission, I successfully advocated for the City of Piedmont to complete a parks master plan. The plan’s conclusions are pretty clear: we’re loving our parks too much, and there is a real need for infrastructure replacements, improvements, and ongoing maintenance to keep our parks welcoming, functional, and sustainable. Park pathways and irrigation systems, in some cases decades old, need priority replacement. Steep slopes in Piedmont and Dracena Parks need erosion mitigation. Costs for all incremental improvements, including ADA upgrades and the replacement of play structures, continue to rise. Measure GG raises badly needed funds, which can help address these needs over time without adding an annual tax burden to city residents. articles.text: As the City Council election approaches, Piedmont Post readers are paying close attention. In a sample of responses from Piedmont Post readers, nearly all, 31 of 33, or 94%, said they plan to vote in November, and 55% said they planned to attend or watch the League of Women Voters candidate forum on Tuesday, Sept. 29. More than 70% of respondents were over 50, a long-tenured and deeply invested local voter base. Readers were asked to pick the three most significant issues facing Piedmont. Five rose to the top: public safety, infrastructure funding, school quality, housing development and city spending. Public safety led the list, cited by 52% of respondents. Readers pointed to pedestrian hazards, traffic enforcement and police staffing. “We do not have enough police service officers. This should be a priority,” one resident wrote. Another described “so many near misses with pedestrians and drivers failing to stop.” Close behind, at 48%, was funding for infrastructure and aging facilities. Residents described potholes, drainage problems, neglected street trees and deferred maintenance across town. “The city has so much deferred maintenance, and we need a source of funding so that it can be addressed,” one resident wrote. School quality ranked third at 45%. School governance is decided in a separate election, but several readers asked council candidates to keep up the long-standing cooperation between the city and the school district on shared facilities. Housing development was named by 42% of readers, driven by state housing mandates and the proposed development in Moraga Canyon. Many were concerned about wildfire evacuation, traffic and the loss of open space in Blair Park. “The Moraga Canyon development will be one of Piedmont’s most consequential land-use decisions in decades,” one resident wrote. Others took a different view: “We need to build more housing to avoid state penalties.” City spending rounded out the top five at 33%, and another 21% chose city and school taxes. Several readers questioned the proposed increase to the real property transfer tax on the November ballot, Measure GG, and asked for more financial transparency. Another asked candidates directly, “How do you control spending while providing the high level of services Piedmont is known for?” With nearly every respondent planning to vote, City Council candidates face an attentive electorate looking for clear, fiscally responsible answers on safety, streets and housing. The Piedmont Post received 33 responses to its online questionnaire Sept. 24-28. Respondents could select up to three issues. articles.text: Editor: The best antidote to screen usage that I can think of is recreation. It is hard to be on a cell phone when you are chasing a soccer ball, blowing bubbles in the pool, or attempting to make a basket. The good news is that we live in a community that prioritizes recreation. Our Piedmont Recreation Department provides all sorts of programming for kids and adults, and helps organize amazing community events like Food Truck Fridays, Movies in the Park, and our beloved Harvest Festival. The not so good news is that we are falling behind on maintaining the very parks, fields, and facilities where these amazing recreational activities take place. Our city employees are working hard with limited funding to prioritize increasingly costly maintenance so that residents can continue to engage in the activities we all enjoy. It is estimated that local Measure GG would provide an additional $1.5 million for the City of Piedmont to help pay for essential services and facilities. Please join me in supporting what we like best about living in Piedmont, please join me in supporting Measure GG. –Chris Hart Piedmont Recreation Commissioner Past President PHS Boosters

articles.text: Claudia Bustos When we picture science, we often picture expertise. A lab. A credential. A specialized instrument. Someone who knows more than we do. Children absorb that image too. Long before they choose a science class or imagine a career, they are forming ideas about who does science, whose knowledge counts, and whether they can see themselves in it. But science has never been an individual pursuit. Knowledge develops through observation, testing, discussion, disagreement, collaboration, and exchange. And it is shaped by something else too: our values, our lived experiences, and our cultures. At The Lawrence Hall of Science, we call this people-powered science. Expertise takes many forms. A biologist, engineer, farmer, artist, educator, parent, or culture bearer may approach the same question differently. People living in a community may recognize change before it appears in a dataset. They see a creek drying up, a neighborhood getting hotter, or the food available nearby beginning to change. Bring those people together and even the questions can change. For children, that opens up a different relationship with STEM. Science becomes less about being the person who already knows the answer and more about noticing carefully, asking questions, sharing what you know, listening to someone who sees something differently, testing an idea, and changing your thinking. At The Lawrence, we want children to meet the people behind the science. In our lobby, they encounter Auntie Dottie, an Ohlone matriarch sharing knowledge about harvesting acorns rooted in this place across generations. In Future of Food, designer and entrepreneur Mónica Martínez introduces visitors to alternative proteins such as mealworms. These are not side stories. They show children that knowledge comes from people, communities, histories, and experience. And with great science comes great responsibility. Alongside “How does this work?” we ask: Who does this affect? Who is missing? Who gets to help decide? Perhaps that is one of the most important STEM identities we can help a child develop: not simply I can do science, but Families explore The Lawrence’s People-Powered Science lobby, where an exhibit developed with Ohlone youth shares cultural knowledge and shows how science is shaped by people, place, and community. The exhibit highlights Auntie Dottie, a matriarch of the East Bay Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone people, as a community science hero.

The Highlanders’ boys’ water polo team got the job done against the visiting Encinal Jets at the Piedmont Pool on Thursday, September 24 in a 14-6 victory. PHS led 12-1 to start the third quarter before rotating out its usual starters, which is a testament to their quality with the Jets entering the match with an 8-1 record. “Encinal’s program is on the up and rising with really good coaching and a lot of club players. So, I’m really proud of the way we executed what we’ve been working on the last couple of weeks,” coach Rik Krumins said. Piedmont has now passed the midway point of its season, holding a 6-6 overall record with seven matches left in its regular season. It was a strong defensive display for the Highlanders on Thursday night against Encinal. It’s something coach Krumins has been looking to instill in his group this season. “We’ve been working on lane defense, counter attack, and knowing when to get to our spots. It really comes out of our defense; we had a game plan to get in the lanes, be aggressive, and be ball hawks. That’s something we’ve talked about all season long,” Krumins said. “Our defense has gotten a lot better; we were a little all over the place on defense or know when to drop. We’ve progressed a ton and have become a lot better. We still need to work on our shot blocking, but other than that, we’re going to be ready to go for WACC and NCS,” sophomore goalie Dylan Jerez mentioned. In water polo, solid defense turns into offensive output. Junior Henry Stein is at the head of that, turning counter attacks into goals. Goalie Dylan Jerez gets his arm on a ball for a save against Encinal. “It starts with the defense. We’re getting the steals, and my goal is to counter out of that and lead our offense down the pool. I’m supposed to be the first one down the pool and being like a quarterback to see what’s there,” Stein said. Match Recap It was a dominant first quarter with Piedmont leading 5-0 through the opening seven minutes. Stein opened the scoring after 52 seconds, then Jack Dahling scored two minutes later when cleaning up his own shot that rebounded off the post. After that, Stein scored after drawing a 5-meter penalty shot with 3:14 to go, and then scored again on an assist from Raffi Banin with 1:58 remaining. Graham Smith then assisted Rylan Patty with 29 seconds left. Encinal scored its first goal 40 seconds into the second quarter, but Piedmont added two more goals in the second to give themselves a 7-1 lead at halftime. They scored via Patty with 4:20 on the clock, and then Jerez hurled a long assist to Stein one minute later. PHS poured on five more unanswered goals in the third quarter to take a commanding 12-1 lead. Piedmont High’s flag football team claimed a come-from-behind 18-6 win over Mt. Eden on Thursday, September 24 at Witter Field. The Highlanders scored all three of their touchdowns in the fourth quarter after trailing 6-0 in the first quarter. “There was no reason for us to be scoreless going into the fourth quarter. Our team needed some time to get it together, but we didn’t collapse, and that’s a win itself,” coach Beth Black said. Piedmont got its first touchdown on an interception returned for a touchdown by Kate Tong with 9:31 left in the fourth. Mt. Eden’s offense relied on stretch runs toward the sidelines, and running back passes from those plays. In the fourth quarter, the Highlanders adjusted, leading to the defense reading it as it happened. “I was playing outside. They were repeating the same play a lot and were sending their blockers out wide. I figured out if I step around their blockers, I could grab it. We definitely watched and learned,” Tong said of the play. Mafi scored a near 40-yard touchdown run with 4:15 left in the game, dodging multiple defenders on her way to the end zone. “We called snake and I knew I wanted the ball. I knew I had to leave the game knowing I did well on both offense and defense. I got the ball, saw my blocks, and kept running until the whistle,” Mafi said. It’s worth noting that Piedmont was credited with a controversial 25-12 loss to Mt. Eden earlier in the season on September 1, where the Monarchs’ varsity squad mistakenly played PHS’ junior varsity team. That result means Piedmont still holds a 6-7 overall and 5-3 against Western Alameda County Conference competition. PHS is disputing the result, but still hasn’t gotten a decision from league officials. “The loss is still there, there hasn’t been a ruling, and they still have that point on us. That stings a lot. I’ve written to the league and we still don’t know what the ruling will be,” Black said. Game Recap Mt. PHS got the job done, claiming a narrow 21-15 victory. Moreau Catholic opened the scoring after starting its first possession at its own 40-yard line. The Mariners moved downfield and connected on a pass over the middle for a touchdown before adding the extra point to take a 7-0 lead. However, the early score did not hurt the Highlanders’ spirits. Fierro returned the following kickoff to Piedmont’s 40-yard line, and a combination of short passes and runs moved the Highlanders into Moreau territory. Quarterback Gio López then connected with Fierro on a 30-yard pass near the goal line, but Moreau forced and recovered a fumble on the next play. Halfway through the second quarter, Diego Garcia jumped a quick out route at the 37-yard line and returned the interception for a touchdown. It marked the second consecutive game in which Piedmont opened its scoring with a pick-six. Ben Gerber added the extra point to tie the game at 7-7. Piedmont’s defense then forced a punt on fourth-and-28 after a key sack from Hildreth pushed Moreau back to its own eight-yard line. Will Dietrick opened the second half with a 51-yard kickoff return to the Moreau 34. Piedmont drove to the 11-yard line before another forced fumble gave the Mariners possession. Moreau capitalized on the turnover, using a combination of short passes and runs to move downfield before a 30-yard reception set up the tying score. The Mariners then converted the two-point attempt to make it 15-15. Dietrick answered with another strong return, and Piedmont again moved into Moreau territory, but the Mariners’ defense held and forced a turnover on downs. Piedmont’s defense responded with key stops of its own, including a pass breakup from Lev Kuluva on a deep fade. Heading into the fourth quarter, Moreau had the ball near its own 40-yard line. A sack from Havea helped force fourth-and-10, where Piedmont’s defense came up with another crucial stop. After Piedmont picked up the first down it needed, Hildreth took a knee to seal the Highlanders’ third consecutive victory, 21-15. Piedmont now enters a bye week before its first league game. articles.text: San Francisco Opera is presenting Scottish composer Thea Musgrave’s Mary, Queen of Scots at the War Memorial Opera House, bringing the 1977 opera back to San Francisco in a new production by director and designer Stewart Laing. “I am thrilled to have my opera Mary, Queen of Scots return to San Francisco Opera this fall,” Musgrave said in a press release. “I have always felt it to be the cornerstone of my operatic repertoire. It is also very close to me personally as I am a woman, a Scot and lived for several years in Paris.” The production, which opened September 20, is a co-production with English National Opera. Italian conductor Clelia Cafiero is making her San Francisco Opera debut leading the San Francisco Opera Orchestra, with soprano Heidi Stober in the title role. Musgrave’s opera centers on the young queen’s struggle to maintain power in Scotland. Three men in Mary’s life, including her half-brother James Stewart, second husband Lord Darnley and future third husband the Earl of Bothwell, each seek to influence or control her reign. The opera combines scenes of political unrest and court intrigue with more intimate moments, including Mary singing a lullaby to her infant son, the future King James I. Musgrave’s opera premiered at the Edinburgh International Festival in 1977. Its U.S. premiere followed in 1978, and Musgrave herself conducted the West Coast premiere at San Francisco Opera’s Spring Opera Theater in 1979. Laing’s production, first presented by English National Opera in 2025, places the story in a contemporary setting and highlights sectarian violence in modern Scotland. D.M. Wood and Mimi Jordan Sherin are the lighting designers, and Colm Seery is the choreographer. Stober returns to the role after performing Mary at London’s Coliseum in 2025. British baritone Thomas Mole makes his American debut as James Stewart, while San Francisco Opera Adler Fellow tenor Thomas Kinch portrays Bothwell. Christopher Sokolowski makes his company debut as Lord Darnley. Baritone Hadleigh Adams portrays the musician and secretary to the queen, David Riccio; bass David Soar is Cardinal Beaton; current Adler Fellow baritone Olivier Zerouali is the Earl of Morton; tenor Chance JonasO’Toole is the Earl of Ruthven; bass-baritone Philip Skinner is Lord Gordon; and Mary’s four eponymous ladies-in-waiting are performed by Adler Fellows Sadie Cheslak (Mary Seton), Sofia Gotch (Mary Beaton), Mary Hoskins (Mary Livingston) and Alexa Frankian (Mary Fleming). Mary, Queen of Scots continues through October 4 at the War Memorial Opera House. For tickets and more information, visit sfopera.com.

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will turn its rooftop sculpture garden into a Korean-pop dance party Thursday, October 15, featuring live performances. “Rooftop Radio: K-pop” will take place from 5:30 to 9 p.m. in the sculpture garden on the museum’s fifth floor. K-pop, short for Korean popular music, encompasses a range of musical styles but is known internationally for elaborate choreography and highly visual performances. The genre has become a major part of American pop culture, with groups such as BTS and BLACKPINK reaching the U.S. mainstream through chart success, sold-out concerts and appearances on American television. SFMOMA’s event will feature sets by Bay Area DJs CAZU, AyumiPlease and Peter Lo, along with performances by local K-pop cover groups Groobeu, K-Pop-Up, Homeground Dance and ECLIPSE. Sassi Fran, a San Francisco-based drag performer and co-founder of K-Pop-Up, will host the performances. The evening also will include a photo booth, toploader decorating and activities from Kloud K-Pop, a South Bay K-pop store. Food and drinks will be available for purchase. The 21-and-over event is part of SFMOMA’s Rooftop Radio series, the museum’s after-hours events combining live music, DJ sets, food, drinks, and late access to museum galleries. Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/event/rooftop-radio-k-pop/ to purchase tickets. The event is part of SFMOMA’s “Rooftop Radio” series. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

articles.text: Tour includes SF dates in November with the San Francisco Symphony Alonzo King LINES Ballet has launched its 2026-27 national tour, bringing four works by San Francisco choreographer Alonzo King to audiences across the country, with San Francisco performances scheduled in November. The tour features LEGACY, King’s recent collaboration with jazz bassist, vocalist and composer esperanza spalding; Ode to Alice Coltrane, a tribute to the composer, pianist and spiritual leader; Ma Mère l’Oye (Mother Goose), set to Maurice Ravel’s score; and Deep River, King’s collaboration with Grammy Award-winning vocalist Lisa Fischer and jazz pianist and composer Jason Moran. The company has several San Francisco performances scheduled this season, including a November 19 through 21 collaboration with the San Francisco Symphony at Davies Symphony Hall. The program will feature world premieres of two ballets choreographed by King to Claude Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune and Aaron Copland’s Appalachian Spring. James Gaffigan will conduct the Symphony. “For more than four decades, touring has been an essential part of the life of LINES Ballet,” King, the company’s founder and artistic director, said in a press release. “Dance is a language that transcends geography and speaks directly to our shared humanity. Every community we visit brings a different energy and perspective to the work. That exchange between artists and audiences is an essential part of why we tour.” Visit www.linesballet.org to purchase tickets. Courtesy of Alonzo King LINES Ballet The tour will showcase four signature works from Alonzo King’s repertoire.

articles.text: September 26 - November 1 Oakland Art Association gallery show Oakland Art Association presents Hopes and Dreams — a curated show that encompasses everyone’s most precious and intimate desires for the future. It can be a dream vacation, a dream come true, a dream for the future of the world or just your part of it. Hope knows no bounds, hope for change, for healing, a brighter future, or for world peace. OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties whose mission is to encourage artistic endeavor in the community, support public school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. Free and open to all! For more information, see www.oaklandart. org. Gallery is open and staffed Saturdays and Sundays from 11 am to 2 pm. Saturday, October 3, 7:00 p.m. Mads Tolling with Kenny Washington Two-time GRAMMY Award-winning Danish jazz violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with prolific pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington. It will be the fourth time the three have performed together. The trio will perform their own music as well as that of composers Chick Corea, Ornette Coleman, and the group Toto, along with songs from the American Songbook, including the Temptations, Carole King, and jazz greats like Thelonious Monk and George Gershwin. Advance tickets are recommended, and are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/jazzviolin; doors open at 6:30 p.m. Tickets are selling rapidly and may well sell out! Friday, October 9, 6:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture A Friday night Extravaganza! Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his home town of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western art. As he moved through his forties, this sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance would continue to yield sculptural masterpieces and explore the art of architecture at San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici family. In 1534, he moved to Rome and only returned to Florence after his passing almost another thirty years later. Doors open at 5:30 p.m. Please bring $20 (cash only) per person to pay for entrance at the door. Saturday, October 10, 7:00 p.m. Virginia Tichenor’s Ragtime Quartet Concert This quartet features ragtime pianist Virginia Tichenor with a stellar line-up of musicians performing ragtime and traditional jazz music. The quartet includes Virginia, of course, Ryan Calloway, clarinet, banjo and vocals; Marty Eggers, tuba, and Robert Young, cornet. Virginia Tichenor is an Oakland-based pianist, originally from St. Louis, MO, the daughter of the late Trebor Tichenor, a noted scholar, pianist and collector of ragtime music. Virginia plays solo piano locally in the Bay Area and is also a traditional jazz pianist, working currently with her husband, Marty Eggers, who also plays with the Zenith, Silver Bell, and Barrelhouse Jazz Bands. Advance tickets are highly recommended for this show, and available now at https://www.ticketsignup.io/ Ragtime. Sunday, October 11, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Mark Williams, and Albert Brooks – will pay tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which fifty or more have become American standards. Van Heusen, although not as well-known as some other American popular music composers, gave us jazz standards such as: Like Someone in Love (1944) and Polka Dots and Moonbeams (1940). He wrote popular music mainly for film and stage. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of an afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Tickets $25 + fee at https://www.ticketsignup.io/JVH, or $30 at the door. Doors open at 4:15 p.m.

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors took a recent excursion, crossing the Bay Bridge for two private group tours, one each of the San Francisco City Hall and the historic James R. Browning United States Federal Building Courthouse. San Francisco City Hall – known as the “People’s Palace” – is the magnificent Beaux-Arts seat of government for the City and County of San Francisco. Reopened in 1915 after the catastrophic destruction of its predecessor in the 1906 earthquake, its iconic dome stands 307 feet tall, making it 42 feet higher than the U.S. Capitol dome! The building has witnessed profound historical moments, including the 1978 assassinations of Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk, and hosted California’s first same-sex marriages in 2004. Speaking of marriages, the City Hall is a very popular venue for weddings, using its elaborate staircase as a backdrop. Several notable public figures and celebrities have been married at San Francisco City Hall, including Marilyn Monroe and Joe DiMaggio, Rosie O’Donnell and Kelli Carpenter, etc. On the morning of the Piedmont Seniors’ visit to City Hall there were several weddings taking place, as well as a couple of quinceañeras. After the City Hall tour the Piedmont Seniors then headed to Max’s Opera Café, an upscale restaurant located in the heart of San Francisco’s Civic Center, which offers classic American fare with an old-school feel and upbeat atmosphere. After lunch the Piedmont Seniors then continued their tour in San Francisco by visiting the James R. Browning United States Courthouse, where they got an in-depth guided tour from John O. Tulloch, retired former Piedmont city clerk and former assistant city administrator. This courthouse has been described as the second most beautiful public building in the United States and was described by Sunset Magazine shortly after its 1905 opening as “A Post Office That’s a Palace.” Today, this historic courthouse is the headquarters of the United States Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. Built in the Beaux-Arts/American Renaissance style, builders used the finest materials and craftsmen to make the building an ode to Greek and Roman architecture. From stained glass skylights to marble columns, with Tiffany glass mosaics to redwood libraries, hand-carved sculptures to hand-tiled floors, the Browning Courthouse is an architectural masterpiece. One of the true highlights of the visit to this building was a visit to Courtroom One, a most elaborate interior space. Originally designed as a trial court and renovated in the 1960s for use by the Court of Appeals, it features marble Corinthian columns and classical symbols of cast-plaster caryatids and cupids. Three ceramic tile mosaics adorn the arched panels. The bench includes Venetian glass motifs, while the wall behind features a decorative design from many colors of marble. It also has marble and plaster representations of 28 different varieties of California fruits and vegetables. All in all, it was a fun-filled, very informative day for the Piedmont Seniors. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov or phone (510) 420-3070. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I know the new iPhones came out, and I have an iPhone 13 and I’d like to update it. The two that I’m the most interested in are the folding phone, or the bigger iPhone Pro. Can you give me an idea of what the differences are? –Sal, Oakland Dear Sal: Yes, it’s that time of year when Apple releases the new iPhone models. Apple has been talking about making a foldable phone for years, and this year, they finally announce the iPhone Duo. The two models that you mentioned; the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the iPhone Duo, really cater to different needs. You can order an iPhone 18 Pro Max or (smaller) 18 Pro now, and in many cases, you can just walk into one of the Apple stores and get one. They have several of the models in stock depending on how much storage you need or what color you want. There will be a non-Pro version of the iPhone 18 probably early next year. As far as the iPhone Duo, you can pre-order that starting on October 16 with availability starting on October 23. Let’s compare the two. First, the iPhone Duo is going to be quite a bit more expensive than the Pro Max starting at around $2000 for 256 GB in storage all the way up to $3200 for 2TB of storage. Compare that to the iPhone 18 Pro Max which starts at $1300 for 256 GB up to $2500 for 2TB. (The smaller 18 Pro costs between $1200 and $2400). The new Duo is made of premium titanium, while the iPhone models are still made with aluminum, which can tend to scratch easily. Since you mentioned that you’re interested in the bigger iPhone Pro Max, the screen size is 6.9 inches. Not quite pocket size, but if you have a thin case, you can fit it in your back pocket. I have the 18 Pro Max, and even with my wallet case I can stick it in my back jeans pocket. It’s bulky, and I can’t really sit down with it in my pocket, but I’m used to that size as I have had the max size since it was available. As in previous models, iPhone 18 Pro is smaller, with a 6.3 inch display. It’s the dual display of the Duo that really makes the biggest difference to user experience. The Duo has a 5.4 inch front display closed and 7.6 inch inner display open. Folded open, it’s like an iPad mini, with more working space than any of the other models. It gives you the opportunity to have more than one app on your screen at a time, with the ability to drag things from one to the other. The big new feature on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is the triple camera set up with variable aperture. Unlike previous iPhones, this one allows you to choose the aperture when taking a shot. While the Duo is no slouch with a 48MP dual fusion camera system, the Pro models blow it out of the water when it comes to photo specs. This is why I decided to get the 18 Pro Max. With the Duo’s inner display, it’s only 31 hours of video playback. These numbers are deceiving because often it depends on what other apps or processes are running on the phone. I have found Apple’s claims of battery life not to be particularly precise, on phones, watches, and laptops. So, who is the iPhone Duo best suited for? If you’re a person who likes to have that newest thing, and don’t mind paying a premium, and you don’t need all of the camera features, then it’s for you. If you want the features of an iPad and iPhone and one device, then it might be worth paying the premium cost for this new iPhone Duo. articles.text: An autumn walk through Piedmont turned into a literary treasure hunt last Wednesday, showing how a shared love of reading can bring a community together step by step. While last Wednesday was the warmest day of the week, weather was no obstacle for our Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. A turnout of 51 walkers and six K-9 companions met at the Exedra to embark on our weekly outing on this crisp first full day of fall. Since July, different participants have taken turns leading the weekly walks. This rotation has highlighted the varied interests and creativity of our members. Last week’s route was designed by June Yee, who invited us to visit four little sidewalk book libraries scattered along a 2.3-mile loop through Piedmont’s scenic neighborhood streets. Walkers were encouraged to bring books to swap or donate. Lois Price, who is currently building an ADU and looking to downsize her personal library, arrived with a generous bag of volumes to distribute along the way. Before setting off, June offered a brief background on the sidewalk library movement. These small, weather-resistant boxes allow neighbors to take or leave books freely. Though informal book sharing has historical roots in older public reading initiatives, today’s widespread sidewalk library phenomenon is remarkably recent. During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, broad efforts emerged to widen book access regardless of income. Philanthropist Andrew Carnegie used his fortune to fund thousands of free public libraries across English-speaking countries. Several local landmarks, such as Oakland’s Temescal Branch, originated as Carnegie libraries. The pioneers of today’s micro-library movement often cite Carnegie’s vision as a primary inspiration. 200 ft · 200 ft June Yee talking to walkers about Sidewalk Libraries Walkers searching for books Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Mary Carter, Nancy Henn, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Jim Kuo, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Charlene Louie, Ken Hubbert, Audrey Sung, Shirley Nakao, Jasmine Cai, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Mike Gallant, Melba Yee, Anne Gritzer, Bern Schild, Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kellogg, Denny McGee, Kristin Howard, Joan Jung with K-9 best friend JT, Bill Ahern, Sherry Jacobs, Judy Wang, June Yee, Debbie Powell, Minoo Clayman, Rich Harms, Vicki Trimbach, Sean Brient with K-9 best friend Pip, Peggy Shultz, Phil Witte, Lois Price, Rick Eigenbrode, Caskey Weston, Stella Houston, Mary Worthington, Chuck Oraftik, Juliane Jacqueline, Stacy Venetluhmamm, Adrienne Hamlin, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, Al Chen with K-9 best friend Sherlock, Brenda Ferrero, Joyce Ahern, Albert Chen, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: A glimpse into the remarkable training of mobility assistance service dogs One of the most well-known types of service dogs is the mobility assistance dog. Organizations such as Canine Companions and Guide Dogs for the Blind are well known for training these amazing dogs, who can dramatically improve the quality of life for their handlers. But very few people understand the vast array of tasks these dogs are able to perform. Fewer still realize that people may qualify for mobility assistance based on their own health-related needs. A well-known area of mobility assistance service dog training is balance and stability tasks. Counterbalance is where the dog provides physical support by walking with steady tension on a rigid harness handle, gently helping to guide the owner should there be a disturbance in their gait or balance. This can be used while walking on flat surfaces, but may be especially helpful when steadying a handler on stairs or while walking uphill. Mobility assistance dogs may also be trained to provide balance support as the handler moves from a seated to a standing position, or vice versa. In this case, the dog acts as a steadying point of contact or counterweight as the handler raises or lowers their body. Although they are not as well known, retrieval and delivery tasks make up an important area of mobility assistance training. Dogs who are able to pick up dropped items may save their owners a great deal of discomfort or improve their safety. Fetching specific items such as a phone, water bottle, or even medication can be extremely important. Many mobility assistance dogs carry items such as medication or water bottles inside specialized vest pockets, but dogs can also be trained to carry specific lightweight items in their mouths for short distances. Finally, certain independence-related tasks help handlers navigate the world more safely. Door and drawer operation means that a dog is trained to pull open doors, drawers, or cabinets using attached fabric pulls, and to close them again with a nose or paw. Dogs may also be trained to press buttons, such as those for automatic doors or light switches. articles.text: One of the pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month and offers movies in a comfortable setting with lively discussion afterwards. The Grand Budapest Hotel, written and directed by Wes Anderson and released to critical acclaim in 2014, is a comedy-drama displaying a wide range of cinematic effects to tell the story of an aging Eastern European hotel through a narrator cast as a writer visiting the hotel in its final days. In the opening scenes, the writer shares his belief that vivid thoughts and memories can’t help but be shared. He begins to learn about the hotel in an interview with the current owner. We are visually transported back in time through the clever use of miniatures in long-distance scenes that are barely noticeable, and varying aspect ratios. They used 1.37:1 for the 1930s, 2.35:1 for the 1960s, and 1.85:1 for the 1980s. Colors in various shades set the mood for the time period being filmed, with unusually rich detailed scenes require the viewer’s full concentration to follow the storyline. Many scenes are perfectly symmetrical, creating visual pairings that emphasize the dialogue taking place between characters. The principal character in this story is the hotel concierge, M. Gustave H., played to perfection by Ralph Fiennes. He reflects on his history with the hotel through whimsical satire, stylized pretension, and nostalgia to alter our perspective from our own current reality. F. Murray Abraham, as Mr. Moustafa, plays the current hotel owner, and is represented in flashbacks as the Lobby Boy, an immigrant fleeing political turmoil before being employed by M. Gustave H. The storyline is linear and a straightforward portrayal of a wealthy dowager’s 20-year affair with the Concierge and the conflicts arising from her desire to leave her estate to him if her death is caused by murder. The dowager’s lawyer, played by Jeff Goldblum, is the center of the controversy involving a forged will fabricated by the dowager’s son, Dimitri, whose role in the dowager’s death leads to suspicion of murder. When the Concierge and Lobby Boy visit the dowager’s estate for a reading of the will, Dimitri conspires to accuse them of her murder and has them arrested and thrown in prison. Their escape from prison, aided by Lobby Boy’s girlfriend, Agatha, and their confrontation with Dimitri unfold in a well-choreographed sequence that reflects the quirky disposition of the dowager’s estate, which includes ownership of the Grand Budapest Hotel. Tragedy arrives in the final scenes with the deaths of the Concierge and Agatha, leaving the Lobby Boy as the surviving owner. The Grand Budapest Hotel will be shown on Thursday, October 8 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free to anyone 18 and over. As a licensed architect with seven years on the Planning Commission working on Piedmont’s Design Guidelines, and four years on City Council, I understand the technical and financial challenges of development. I know our obligation to meet state housing requirements while making sure city-owned land serves Piedmont’s broader community needs. I will evaluate the proposed partner against the RFQ criteria, the Specific Plan, our fiscal realities, and community commitments. I will vote yes only if the agreement is specific, financially credible, and aligns with the MCSP. Sunny Bostrom-Fleming Several years ago, I placed an offer to purchase a home on Moraga Ave. The offer was accepted, subject to inspections, and they turned out positive. Then, two days before closing escrow, the house started to slide. Inside, the marble counters in the kitchen separated from the back wall. The hillside-facing walls separated from the hardwood floors. An independent engineer did an inspection and said this whole area is a mudslide area, and the proposed soccer field stadium will not work in this area. I decided to run for City Council to make sure the word got out about the dangers of the soccer project and the mudslides. Finally, just before the final council vote to approve the soccer field on Moraga Ave, there was a mudslide, closing Moraga Ave for 2 days, as I had predicted. We need massive community input to ensure that if this area is developed, the city aligns our history and our vision for the future, keeping our citizens, our children, our pets, and wildlife safe. Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is part of the Housing Element mandated by the State of California for all cities. A few cities resisted their housing mandates and exposed themselves to litigation, fines, and penalties, including the loss of control over zoning decisions. One consequence of non-compliance is the state-imposed “Builder’s Remedy,” which allows developers to choose where and what to build without resident input. I am grateful to our city leaders for their determination to keep Piedmont in compliance. The Specific Plan is a comprehensive vision developed with city staff leadership and considerable public input. The plan envisions design, landscaping, traffic circulation, pedestrian safety, wildfire mitigation, storm drainage, geological studies, financing, and other details. The plan is available for review on Piedmont’s Planning & Building Department website. The Specific Plan was used to issue Requests for Interest to prospective developers. If one or more developers express interest in this project, proposals and qualifications would be evaluated for adherence to the plan. I am interested in ensuring a developer’s financial viability and track record in delivering similar projects. My focus would be on public safety, traffic circulation, emergency evacuation, pedestrian and bicycle safety, and wildfire mitigation. Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I support creating new and affordable housing. Throughout my career at the Attorney General’s Office, I advocated for equitable, accessible, and affordable housing. Where you live impacts so many aspects of your life — where you work and buy food, public safety, transportation, your friends and neighbors, and your schools. At the same time, Piedmont is required to plan for hundreds of new homes in a city with little undeveloped land. Meeting that state housing obligation will require thoughtful planning and difficult choices. Any development needs to reflect both our housing obligations and the needs of the Piedmont community.

articles.text: Editor: It gives me great pleasure to highly recommend Adam Hundt for the Piedmont City Council. Adam is a leader who understands the issues impacting our daily quality of life: safety, community spaces, and preserving our green environments. As a father with young children, he also recognizes long-term challenges, particularly the climate crisis. Adam knows every community must contribute to robust climate action by accelerating home and vehicle electrification and using public facilities for clean energy. These actions will boost our quality of life, improve property values, and secure a better future. The city understands the climate work ahead. In 2025, the Planning Department created the Award for Sustainable Home Design and Construction. I was honored to be one of the inaugural winners for fully electrifying our home. However, there is much more to do. Adam will invigorate Piedmont’s climate plan to help us realize these goals. Please visit Adam’s webpage (AdamHundt.com) and invest in Piedmont’s future by giving him your vote. –James Glauber, MD, MPH

articles.text: On September 24, Piedmont Police announced a significant update in a case that led to the arrest of multiple suspects and the seizure of illegally possessed items. In August, Sergeant Kristina Foster conducted a traffic stop that led to the discovery of two firearms concealed inside the vehicle’s engine compartment and the arrest of a suspect. Sgt. Foster continued to follow up on the investigation with members of the police department, leading to the arrest and a search warrant at the suspect’s residence. The department worked with the Oakland Police Department and California Highway Patrol Air Unit to safely execute the search warrant at the suspect’s residence, where they seized guns, ammunition, and weapons. The suspect was taken into custody and booked at Santa Rita Jail without incident. “This case is a great example of the work that continues long after an initial arrest, following leads, developing information, and working collaboratively with our law enforcement partners to keep our communities safe,” said the Piedmont Police Department in a statement released on their Facebook page.
